answer: Latency triangulation stops one machine faking a crowd. Three landmarks on three continents form a triangle, each a vertex, and each fires a random nonce at once. The agent signs all three and sends them back while each landmark times the trip. A real agent sits inside the triangle, so its times match its claimed spot. A farm in one datacenter shows the same delay everywhere, which exposes it. Faking 1,000 agents in 1,000 places needs 1,000 machines on real networks, about $180,000 a year. It is a velvet rope at a garden gate: one ticket, one guest, and nobody can clone the queue.
